title: Which AI can generate a full 3D scene or game level, not just objects?
author: St4rgazer7
selftext:
Discussions on AI-based 3D generation tend to focus on individual elements like characters, furniture, or props.

But I'm interested to know if AI is able to generate complete 3D scenes or game levels.

For instance, what if I wanted to describe a scene of a medieval village showing houses, roads, trees, and rolling terrain, and perhaps a central marketplace? I’m interested to know if I could get a response in the form of a structured 3D scene that can be opened, for example, in Blender or a game engine.

World models feel relevant to this. For example, some companies are doing research in spatially-consistent and interactive environments.

However, generating a scene that can be explored is different from generating a level that can be edited, which involves generating and organizing various meshes, materials, collisions, and navigation.

There are other aspects of a game engine that still need to be modeled, for example, audio sources.

Tripo studio offers image-to-text and text-to-3D asset generation, which could be used to create elements of a larger scene.

Maybe an improvement would be a combination of an AI asset generator with a scripting agent in Blender, or some other procedural generator, to ensure consistency in style, size, and overall usability of the environment.

For game development, I would want to generate a scene with collision meshes, optimized models, and a clear scene hierarchy that developers can work with.

Is there an AI workflow that can do this?

"There's a reason modular design exist ,
 make many props and build your scenes like Lego "


That way you are able to cull individual objects when needed to not mess up another person's gpu or cpu 


Yours

Not even to talk about how little interactive elements you can add in your case of what you want.

comments.author: Talongar
comments.body:
You could in theory yes probably brute force this with the right prompting and outline. 
But it would be wildly inefficient in both performance and token cost. In my amateur opinion.

Depending on your use case. 
A better method I think would be to first tackle a procedural generator and then generate the individual elements for the scene kit and run the generator. 

That way if something doesn't look right you can tweak the generators algorithm instead of burning tokens generating iterations of full complex meshes.
